https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.question: Does intelligence require a brain, or can adaptive behavior itself count as cognition?
https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.thesis: One side argues that flexible, history-sensitive problem-solving in organisms such as slime moulds warrants a broad biological concept of cognition; critics insist the term must be narrow enough to discriminate among mechanisms.
https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.argument: Slime moulds respond to gradients, alter networks and sometimes exploit traces of prior movement. Proponents treat these capacities as primitive cognition; skeptics argue chemical feedback can explain them without invoking mental states.
https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.intellectual_background: The debate contrasts nervous-system-centered theories with embodied, distributed and biogenic approaches to mind; defining intelligence by human-like reasoning would beg the question.
https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.example: A slime mould's route through a maze may improve after repeated exploration even though it has no neurons.
https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.strongest_objection: If every adaptive process is called intelligent, the term loses explanatory force; a thermostat could qualify.
https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.possible_response: Proponents can specify degrees of adaptive control, memory and environmental sensitivity, then test whether the framework predicts new behavior.
https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.implications: Definitions influence which organisms are studied and which experiments count as tests of learning.
